newsitem.title: GERMANY: German ministers air opposing views on NATO.
newsitem.headline: German ministers air opposing views on NATO.

text.p: German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said on Sunday the first wave of NATO's expansion should be limited to three members even though Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said Bonn could support adding five.

Speaking to ZDF television before the NATO summit in Madrid on Tuesday, Ruehe said he favoured the U.S. position on NATO's eastern enlargement because the alliance could run into difficulties if the first wave were too large.

"There are not five but 12 states wanting to enter NATO and there is no way we could take in all 12 at once," Ruehe said. "That is why I favour starting with a small group. That would be easier for NATO to digest.
"That would also be the strongest signal that the first admitted will not be the last and that the door will not be closing," he added.

Germany, whose position could be decisive in Madrid, has remained officially noncommital about the size of eastern enlargement even as many European states lined up behind France in calling for NATO to extend membership offers to five formerly communist states.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to be invited to join the 16-nation North Atlantic Treaty Organisation at the summit.
But Many European NATO members want Slovenia and Romania included even though the United States has firmly stated it wants to limit the first enlargement to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Kinkel said earlier on Sunday the German government could support a larger NATO expansion to include four or five new members.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl has said Germany supports the bids of Romania and Slovenia, but has avoided any public promise to either nation that they should be included in the first wave.

The opposing views expressed on Sunday by Kinkel and Ruehe reflect a long-held split on the issue within the Bonn government, but was the first time the two had carried out their campaigns in such a public manner.
Ruehe is a member of Kohl's Christians Democrats (CDU) and Kinkel is a member of the liberal Free Democrats (FDP), junior coalition partners in Kohl's three-party government.
"The decision is still open," Kinkel told the Welt am Sonntag newspaper. "It will be exciting in Madrid."
Kinkel said that just because the U.S. had taken a position limiting the enlargement to three nations that did not mean a final decision has already been made.

"The (German) government could support a larger enlargement of four or five new members," Kinkel said. "The alliance decisions are always a consensus. Germany's open position is oriented towards finding a consensus."
Kinkel said Germany was heading to the summit confident that there would be a compromise.
